title: Freshwater mussels (mukirr)

names.gloss: mussel, found in fresh and brackish water

identification.basis: The dictionary's mukirr is the freshwater mussel, with the cooking method. The Australian Museum holds Velesunio angasi from the Mitchell River a few kilometres from the Karma Waters homestead, and the Atlas of Living Australia has four records within 30 km.

summary: **[mukirr](word:mukirr)** is the mussel: 'found in fresh and brackish water. There are many up the Daintree near Bairds, some up Granite Creek. Has to be cleaned from the black stuff that tastes like tobacco. First roast it, then clean the "ear" out, then boil it or else eat it right away without boiling' [ref:hershberger1982]. The river mussel of the north is *Velesunio angasi*, 'a shallow burrower in silty sand/mud in streams, billabongs, and slow-flowing rivers', a suspension feeder that breeds through the year and broods its larvae in its gills [ref:lucid-velesunio]. It is the easiest meat in the river, dug by hand from the sand of the pools and roasted in the ashes, which is how Roth says 'the large majority of these shell-fish' were cooked, by the women who 'generally' prepared 'yams, roots, nuts, and shell-fish' [ref:roth1901]. The shell was a tool as well: a scoop and spoon, an ash-scraper and a cutter, and on the Mitchell the blade that scraped the [bloodwood](entry:bloodwood) manna and the inner bark of the string plants [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904] [ref:palmer1883].

infobox.label: The animal
infobox.value: Velesunio angasi: a compressed, elongate shell with a winged back end; a shallow burrower in silty sand and mud; filter feeder; breeds all year, larvae brooded in the gills

infobox.label: Where
infobox.value: Pools, billabongs and slow reaches of the Mitchell; Australian Museum specimens from near the homestead

infobox.label: Cooking
infobox.value: Roast, clean out the 'ear' (the black part that tastes of tobacco), then boil or eat

infobox.label: The shell
infobox.value: Scoop, spoon, scraper, cutter; manna-scraper and bark-scraper on the Mitchell

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[mukirr](word:mukirr)** 'mussel' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth recorded the river mussel (*Unio*) as *wambiram* on the Pennefather and the Cape Bedford scoop made from it as *warboparka*; his list of edible molluscs runs to pages, nearly all of them sea shells with Pennefather, Cape Bedford and Bloomfield names [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1904]. The shell tools have their own words: **[warkal](word:warkal)** the [bailer shell](entry:bailer-shells) billy and **[jurungurr](word:jurungurr)** 'spoon made in old time' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The mussel
sections.body:
*Velesunio angasi* was named *Unio angasi* by Sowerby in 1867 from the Strangways River in the Northern Territory. 'The shell is compressed, relatively elongate, the posterior expanded, usually winged'. It is a 'shallow burrower in silty sand/mud in streams, billabongs, and slow-flowing rivers', a 'suspension feeder'; 'reproduction occurs throughout the year', and the larvae, glochidia, 'are brooded in the marsupia', the gill pouches, before they attach to a host fish [ref:lucid-velesunio]. 'This species is widely distributed, occurring from north-eastern Queensland throughout tropical northern Australia, and extending south to the Pilbara region of Western Australia' [ref:lucid-velesunio].

The one long study of the animal was done on Magela Creek in Kakadu, 'a seasonally flowing stream of tropical northern Australia' like the Mitchell: 'shell shape and environment, distribution, abundance, population dynamics, reproduction, food ingestion, physiological condition, production, and seasonal changes in any of these' [ref:humphrey1985]. Because it filters the water and lives for years in one place, the same mussel is used across the north as a monitor of metals and radium in the water, which is also a reason to be careful what water you take it from [ref:lucid-velesunio].

The dictionary's note that it 'has to be cleaned from the black stuff that tastes like tobacco' is the one piece of cooking advice recorded in Kuku Yalanji: roast, open, clean out the 'ear', then boil or eat [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Mussel, cockle, baler
sections.body:
- **The river mussel** (*mukirr*, *Velesunio*): dark, elongate, winged at the back, in fresh water sand and mud [ref:lucid-velesunio] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **The mangrove cockle** (*Geloina coaxans*), which Anderson's informants used the same way as scrapers and cutters, is a thick estuary shell [ref:anderson1996].
- ***Cyrena***, the thick estuary cockle whose edge cut bark [ref:roth1904].
- **The baler** (*warkal*): the sea volute that became a pot; see [bailer shells](entry:bailer-shells) [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Empty shells on the bottom** are turtle work, not a sign of a dead bed [ref:turtle-competition].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Slits in the sand** of a pool's shallows, the mussel's siphons showing; a hand run through the sand finds them [ref:lucid-velesunio].
- **Piles of opened shells on a bank** are birds and water rats; shells opened on the bottom are turtles; see the [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher] [ref:turtle-competition].
- **Middens** of mussel shell on an old camp terrace are heritage and are left [ref:acha2003].
- **A shrinking pool** in the late dry concentrates the mussels into the last wet sand [ref:humphrey1985].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body: 'Silty sand/mud in streams, billabongs, and slow-flowing rivers': the sandy pools and backwaters, not the fast rock runs [ref:lucid-velesunio]. The [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page gives the pools' year.

sections.heading: The mussel in the pool
sections.body: The mussel filters the pool, lives in it for years, and is eaten by the [freshwater turtles](entry:freshwater-turtle), the water rat and the birds; its larvae ride the gills of the pool's fish, so a pool without fish has no young mussels [ref:lucid-velesunio] [ref:turtle-competition]. It is the dry-season food of the shrinking pool, with the [lilies](entry:water-lilies), the [cherabin](entry:cherabin) and the [catfish](entry:catfish) that share the bottom [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Mussels breed through the year and are there in every season, but they are gathered when the water is low and warm and the sand is within reach: the dry, from the end of the wet to the first storms [ref:lucid-velesunio] [ref:bom-palmerville]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Food**, roasted in the ashes, then cleaned and boiled or eaten [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
- **Scoops and spoons** from the unmodified valve [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
- **Scrapers**, 'to remove ashes from cooked meat', and **cutters**; only from live shells, 'as dead ones cracked unevenly when worked' [ref:anderson1996].
- **Manna and bark scrapers** on the Mitchell [ref:palmer1883].
- **A pelican lure** at Boulia: empty shells thrown onto the water to mimic jumping fish [ref:roth1901].
- **Bait** for the [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines).

sections.heading: Gathering and cooking mukirr
sections.body:
From the dictionary and Roth [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Find the bed** in the sandy shallows of a pool or backwater; feel through the sand with your fingers or toes for the shells standing on edge [ref:lucid-velesunio].
2. **Gather** into a bag or trough; take the bigger ones and leave the small [ref:anderson1996].
3. **Roast** them in the ashes until they open [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
4. **Clean out the 'ear'**, the black part 'that tastes like tobacco' [ref:hershberger1982].
5. **Boil** the cleaned meat, or eat it 'right away without boiling' [ref:hershberger1982].
6. **Keep the shells**: a live-taken valve is a scoop, a scraper and a knife [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- A filter feeder takes up what is in the water; mussels from a fouled, stagnant or mine-affected pool are a bad idea, which is why they are used as pollution monitors [ref:lucid-velesunio].
- Crocodile water: feel for mussels in the daytime in open shallows, with someone watching [ref:crocwise] [ref:kw-about].
- Middens are heritage; take live shells only [ref:acha2003].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Mussels are still in the rivers on both sides of the range; see each place below for where they are recorded. Freshwater shellfish on native title country are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* and the Aboriginal-use provisions of the *Fisheries Act 1994* [ref:alrc] [ref:qld-fishact]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission.

locations.summary: Mussels are a food of the Hann's country. A Thaypan man told the Federal Court that on Thaypan country, which takes in the Hann, 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan]. The written record of the animal itself is thin: the Atlas of Living Australia holds one freshwater mussel record, *Velesunio angasi* in 2000, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: The Hann is a sandy, spring-fed river that has not had a day without flow since its gauge was put in in 1968 [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby] [ref:bom-105001b]. The mussel lives in 'silty sand/mud in streams, billabongs, and slow-flowing rivers' [ref:lucid-velesunio], so look in the sandy pools and backwaters, not the fast runs. Lagoons and swamps are one of the nine kinds of country the Kuku Thaypan Elders name [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: From December to March the rivers flood out over the plains [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Hann runs lowest from September to November, a low, clear run between deep holes [ref:bom-105001b]. That is when the sandy shallows are easiest to reach, and when crocodiles are in the same holes; see [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles).

sections.heading: How people dealt with them here
sections.body:
**Mussels and law.** In the Kuku Thaypan Elders' law there are story places where girls must not eat mussels, 'as to do so may harm the health of their babies' [ref:standley2019]. The places and their stories belong to the Elders' families and are not named here.

**Fewer and smaller.** The Elders say mussels 'were once larger and in high number across the entire wetland complex'. In their plan for a lagoon on Kuku Thaypan country, the signs of healthy country include the 'Return of mussel numbers and size', along with keeping cattle and pigs out to stop the 'trampling and muddying of edge of lagoon' [ref:standley2019]. Feral pigs 'occur in large numbers' in Rinyirru [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country and the upper Hann is the Possum People's country. Their November 2023 determinations recognise rights to hunt, fish and gather on the land and waters [ref:fca-thaypan] [ref:fca-possum]. Others need the Traditional Owners' permission.

locations.summary: In the Mitchell at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the mussel is *Velesunio angasi*, and the Australian Museum has specimens from the river near the homestead [ref:ala-mussel].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: The sandy pools and backwaters of the Mitchell, not the fast rock runs [ref:lucid-velesunio]. The Australian Museum holds specimens from the Mitchell River just below the [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) homestead, and the Atlas has four records within 30 km [ref:ala-mussel] [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The mussels are in the Mitchell at Karma Waters now, recorded within a few kilometres of the homestead, and the dictionary's cooking note is complete enough to follow this afternoon [ref:ala-mussel] [ref:hershberger1982]. The station's river camps are on the pools where the beds are [ref:kw-camping].

locations.summary: On the coast the dictionary records mukirr in the rivers of the Daintree side [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: The dictionary puts them 'in fresh and brackish water', up the Daintree and Granite Creek on the east side [ref:hershberger1982].
